sessions.session_name: Case Challenge: Leading in Times of Change

magic_moments.quote: We are living in this world of AI. We can calculate break-even costs in a second on our computers. We could probably even build a really complex financial model in moments. So why even think about finance? Because it still needs human judgment — to understand the numbers, to understand why the decisions are being made, and to pressure test my assumptions.
magic_moments.why_magic: Tam names the elephant in the room before participants can. If AI can do the math, why are we here? She reframes the value proposition of the entire session in one breath, landing it on judgment and pressure-testing assumptions — which is exactly what the case will demand of them.

magic_moments.context: Just before launching the first breakout
magic_moments.quote: Your job is to try things and make mistakes and see how you can figure it out. Failure actually is the goal here in order to learn and grow from it.
magic_moments.why_magic: She gives explicit permission to fail right before the first decision the teams have to make. Participants who feel safe taking risks engage more deeply — and the data later in the chapter (teams who tried bold paths got the best feedback) bears this out.

magic_moments.context: Mid-debrief, bridging the simulation back to participants' real work
magic_moments.quote: Our time here is not well spent if we're not … like I've said in every session, our job is to provide seeds for you to extrapolate and pull back into your world.
magic_moments.why_magic: She makes the meta-purpose of the session explicit, mid-flow. The simulation isn't the point — the point is what participants can take back to BD. Naming that out loud reshapes how participants engage with the rest of the debrief.

facilitators.name: Nick White

magic_moments.context: Debriefing a team that took a bold position with senior leaders
magic_moments.quote: Without risk, we don't get rewards. There's nothing wrong with talking about risk, there's nothing wrong with presenting risk, even having high risk — if we can articulate the upside.
magic_moments.why_magic: Nick reframes risk from a thing to hide from leadership into a thing to *present* to leadership. For managers heading into real budget conversations, that's the unlock — it's not the risk that kills the proposal, it's the failure to articulate the upside.

magic_moments.context: Opening minute with a finance-fluent cohort
magic_moments.quote: When you go on a training and it's stuff you already know, you think, you know, what on earth am I doing here? But actually, by turning it around, that can be really quite powerful for you.
magic_moments.why_magic: He pre-empts the disengagement risk in a room full of finance people who could teach this content themselves. The frame: your job is to teach — which is harder than learning — and that's how mastery shows up.

magic_moments.quote: We believe in bringing the real world in. So, we're gonna try and bring in as much of the real world as possible. Relate what we're learning back to BD. This is actually quite a challenging way of learning. It's actually a really powerful way of learning, because…
magic_moments.why_magic: Right at the start of the program, Nick sets the contract: the cases will feel uncomfortable because they're trying to mirror BD's real complexity, and that discomfort is the point. Participants who buy into that contract in minute 11 engage differently for the rest of the journey.

magic_moments.transcript_path: Kickoff - Get the Message/05.05.26 - Kickoff GTM - Tara/GMT20260505-151546_Recording.transcript.vtt
magic_moments.context: Setting up Jamie, the first AI character participants will meet
magic_moments.quote: Your interaction is going to be your live conversation with Jamie. You'll be able to ask questions, explore what's really going on, and help her think through the options. So, in this opportunity to learn, it is thinking alongside a peer around how to approach this problem of a culture of always-on.
magic_moments.why_magic: Tara frames the AI character as a thinking partner, not a chatbot to interrogate. That micro-reframe — peer vs. quiz — sets a different tone for the whole conversation that follows.

magic_moments.transcript_path: Kickoff - Get the Message/05.05.26 - Kickoff GTM - Tara/GMT20260505-151546_Recording.transcript.vtt
magic_moments.context: Briefing teams just before they go into the breakout
magic_moments.quote: What you're gonna do in this conversation is pull on your natural instincts, your experiences as a leader, but then also draw from some of your learning from Leading with Impact.
magic_moments.why_magic: She links the AI conversation to two anchors at once: lived experience and prior program content. Participants who hold both at the same time give Jamie better counsel — and they discover something about their own decision-making in the process.

magic_moments.context: Sharing a personal leadership story during the framing chapter
magic_moments.quote: The abrupt loss of a boss was more deeply emotional than I initially anticipated, and so I took a moment, and just sat with everybody, one-on-one, and heard them. And that was the most important thing to do.
magic_moments.why_magic: Tara models the move she's asking participants to practice — slow down, sit with people, lead emotionally — by telling on herself first. Vulnerability from the facilitator earns vulnerability from the room.

magic_moments.quote: The real human component of this is difficult to bring into play when you're dealing with non-humans. A huge strength across the board was you all were really being strategic around the additional capabilities that were possible through this reorg, and really being able to connect and align the operations.
magic_moments.why_magic: She holds two truths together: the AI conversation is necessarily limited on human-ness, AND the participants were strategic in spite of that. The debrief gives credit and surfaces the limit of the modality in the same breath.

facilitators.name: Rebecca Kaloo

sessions.session_name: Case Challenge: Leading in Times of Change

magic_moments.quote: What absolutely fascinates me is that, despite having fantastic strategies, despite having really great grip on the numbers, actually, for organisations to do their really best work — to be able to grow in the ambitious way that you want to be growing — requires fantastic leadership skills.
magic_moments.why_magic: Rebecca opens with curiosity rather than authority — "what fascinates me" — and lands the case for leadership as the limiting reagent. She makes the rest of the session feel like an exploration she's hosting, not a lecture she's delivering.

magic_moments.context: Debrief after the second breakout — calling out peer learning
magic_moments.quote: That idea of exchanging perspectives, and just how powerful and really useful it is to get those different perspectives and have that challenge as well. Leslie, I can see you were nodding along there, so I'm gonna drag you in…
magic_moments.why_magic: Rebecca catches a moment of peer learning happening in real time and elevates it as the lesson. The drag-Leslie-in move is what separates a facilitator from a presenter — she runs toward the energy in the room.
